sections.name: Booklet A · Vocabulary Cloze
sections.passage: Our school field was closed for six weeks in June. The grass had worn away in the middle, and the ground underneath had become so (1)______ that it was no longer safe to run on. New turf was laid, and orange cones were placed around the (2)______ so that nobody would walk across it. Most of us (3)______ about this at first, because recess suddenly felt very small. By the time the field reopened in August, however, the grass was thick and even, and the first game of captain's ball was (4)______ enough to be worth the wait. Mr Lee, who had argued for the repair for two years, said nothing at all, but we noticed that he came out to (5)______ that afternoon.

sections.name: Booklet B · Grammar Cloze
sections.instruction: Fill each blank with one suitable word.
sections.passage:
The Lost Shoe

On the first day of the holidays, my cousin Farid lost one shoe in the sea at Changi.

He (1)______ standing in the water up to his knees when a wave knocked him over. By the time he stood up again, the left shoe (2)______ gone. We searched for almost an hour, walking up and down the shallow water, (3)______ we never found it.

Farid had to walk back to the car park with one shoe (4)______ and one shoe off, which his sister found far funnier (5)______ he did.

That evening his mother said she (6)______ not going to buy a new pair until September, because the old ones (7)______ almost too small anyway.

Farid spent the rest of the holidays in his school shoes. He (8)______ complained at all. But on the last Sunday, (9)______ we went back to the same beach, he left both shoes in the car and walked to the water barefoot, (10)______ a person who has learnt something.

answers.tip: 'He' is singular and the action was going on: was standing.
'Had gone' or 'was gone' both work here.
The two ideas disagree, so 'but' is needed.
'One shoe on and one shoe off' is the set pair.
'Funnier' is a comparative, so it takes 'than'.
Reported speech: she said she was not going to.
'He never complained at all' — the negative is needed before the verb.
'Like a person who has learnt something' makes the comparison.

sections.name: Booklet B · Editing
sections.instruction: There is one spelling or grammar error in each numbered line. Write the correction — one word only.

questions.q: Our class has been collecting old newspaper since April.
questions.tip: The error was “newspaper”. More than one is collected, so the plural is needed.

questions.q: Each pupil bring a bundle from home every Monday.
questions.tip: The error was “bring”. 'Each pupil' is singular.

questions.q: We tie them with string and stack them neatly in the coridor.
questions.tip: The error was “coridor”. It has two r's.

questions.q: The bundles are then wieghed on a scale borrowed from the canteen.
questions.tip: The error was “wiegh”. It is spelt w-e-i-g-h-e-d.

questions.q: Last month we collected more paper then any other class.
questions.tip: The error was “then”. After a comparative use 'than'.

questions.q: Mrs Ong was very pleased of the result.
questions.tip: The error was “of”. The phrase is 'pleased with'.

questions.q: The money from the paper are used to buy books for the library.
questions.tip: The error was “are”. The subject is 'the money', which is singular.

questions.q: So far we have bought eleven new books, including three atlas.
questions.tip: The error was “atlas”. The plural is 'atlases'.

questions.q: My favourite is a book about heros who explored the Arctic.
questions.tip: The error was “heros”. The plural is 'heroes'.

questions.q: I have read it three times allready.
questions.tip: The error was “allready”. It has one l: al-ready.

questions.q: Next term we will started collecting bottles as well.
questions.tip: The error was “started”. After 'will' the plain verb is used.

questions.q: Mrs Ong says that bottles are worth more then paper.
questions.tip: The error was “then”. After a comparative use 'than'.

sections.name: Booklet B · Synthesis and Transformation
sections.instruction: Rewrite each sentence using the word given. The meaning must stay the same. Each question is worth 2 marks.

questions.q: The box was very heavy. Farid could not lift it. **(too)**
questions.m: The box was too heavy for Farid to lift

questions.q: "I am bringing the tickets," said Priya. **(that)**
questions.m: Priya said that she was bringing the tickets

questions.q: The rain was heavy. We stayed indoors. **(so … that)**
questions.m: The rain was so heavy that we stayed indoors

sections.name: Booklet B · Comprehension
sections.instruction: Read the passage and answer the questions. Note the marks for each question.
sections.passage:
The Quiet Shop

There is a bookshop near my aunt's flat that has a sign on the door reading NO TALKING, PLEASE. It is not a library. It is a shop, and things in it are for sale.

The owner, Mr Pillai, is not unfriendly. He nods when you come in and nods when you leave. If you need to ask him something, you write it on one of the small yellow squares of paper beside the till, and he writes back underneath.

My aunt says he has run the shop that way for eleven years, and that when he first put the sign up, customers stopped coming. For six months the shop was nearly empty.

Then something changed. People who wanted to be left alone began to travel there on purpose — from other estates, and then from other parts of the island. A newspaper wrote about it. Now the shop is busier on a Saturday than any bookshop in the mall, and it is completely silent.

The first time my aunt took me, I found it uncomfortable. I kept wanting to say something about a book I had found, and there was nobody to say it to. I bought nothing and was glad to leave.

The second time, I stayed for two hours.

What changed was a girl of about six at the shelf by the window. She had found a book about sharks and was holding it open with both arms because it was too big for her hands. She did not say anything. She simply turned it round and showed it to me, and I nodded, and she went back to reading. The whole exchange took four seconds and I have remembered it for three years.

I do not think the sign is really about noise. I think Mr Pillai worked out that most of us have nowhere at all to go where nothing is expected of us, and that this is worth more than conversation.

I have written him two notes in three years. He has answered both. I still do not know what his voice sounds like.

questions.q: What is unusual about the sign on the door of the shop?
questions.a: It says NO TALKING, PLEASE, which is what you would expect in a library rather than in a shop where things are for sale.

questions.q: How does Mr Pillai answer a customer's question?
questions.a: The customer writes the question on a small yellow square of paper beside the till, and Mr Pillai writes his reply underneath it.

questions.q: What happened to the shop in the first six months after the sign went up?
questions.a: Customers stopped coming and the shop was nearly empty.

questions.q: Give two ways in which we know the shop later became successful.
questions.a: Any two of: people travelled there on purpose from other estates and other parts of the island; a newspaper wrote about it; it is now busier on a Saturday than any bookshop in the mall.

questions.q: Why did the narrator find the first visit uncomfortable?
questions.a: He kept wanting to say something about a book he had found, and there was nobody he was allowed to say it to.

questions.q: How do we know the narrator's opinion of the shop changed?
questions.a: On the first visit he bought nothing and was glad to leave, but on the second visit he stayed for two hours.

questions.q: Which two-word phrase in the passage means 'deliberately'?
In your own words, explain what the narrator thinks the sign is really for.
questions.a: He thinks it is not about noise at all. He believes Mr Pillai realised that most people have nowhere to go where nothing at all is expected of them, and that having such a place matters more than being able to talk.

questions.q: What does the last sentence tell us about how the narrator and Mr Pillai know each other?
questions.a: They have exchanged two written notes over three years, but the narrator has never heard Mr Pillai speak. It shows that they have got to know each other without a single spoken word.
